articles.title: One Hundred and Thirty Hindu Americans Walked Into Congress on the Fourth of July Eve. Seven Lawmakers Walked Out Allies.
articles.excerpt: CoHNA's fifth Hindu Advocacy Day drew bipartisan support from both parties on Capitol Hill, blending the celebration of America's 250th birthday with an urgent pushback against rising Hinduphobia.
articles.image_caption: The United States Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., where Hindu American delegates gathered for their fifth annual advocacy day
articles.nri_angle: Hindu Americans are building serious political muscle — 130 delegates from 15 states descended on Capitol Hill, held 50-plus meetings with Senate and House staff, visited 120 offices, and secured bipartisan condemnation of temple attacks. This is diaspora civic engagement maturing from protest to policy.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Long Island's India Day Parade Turns Fifteen. The Guest List Now Includes State Senators.
articles.excerpt: The curtain raiser for the 15th India Day Parade USA packed 250 people into a government building in Mineola — a far cry from the modest procession that started the tradition in 2011.
articles.image_caption: Indian tricolor flags waving during a patriotic celebration
articles.nri_angle: What began as a small community parade on Long Island has grown into a celebration so large it draws state senators, county comptrollers, and Indian consular officials — a measure of how deeply Indian Americans have woven themselves into suburban New York's civic fabric.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A New Jersey Temple Has Screened 15,000 People for Free. Now It Wants to Become a Permanent Clinic.
articles.excerpt: Health Camp of New Jersey, a volunteer-run nonprofit housed in the Balaji Temple in Bridgewater, is preparing to transform from an annual health fair into a year-round Federally Qualified Health Center.
articles.image_caption: A Hindu temple in New Jersey — community health camps at temples have screened over 15,000 people for chronic diseases since 1999 (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian American temples are evolving from spiritual centres into critical community health infrastructure, filling gaps left by the US insurance system for underserved South Asian populations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: They Read the News from Memory, Without Teleprompters. Now a New York Library Is Making Sure the Diaspora Remembers.
articles.excerpt: The Indian Diaspora Center's annual symposium brought Doordarshan veterans and digital-age journalists under one roof in Elmont, New York, to document a media revolution that shaped how millions of Indians — at home and abroad — understood their country.
articles.image_caption: Doordarshan Bhavan in New Delhi — a New York symposium is preserving the golden era of Indian television for the diaspora (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: A New York–based diaspora centre is building a permanent archive of Indian community history, using events like this symposium to document the cultural touchstones — Doordarshan chief among them — that connected generations of NRIs to home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indiaspora Just Catalogued 250 Milestones of Indian American Life. The Timing Is Not a Coincidence.
articles.excerpt: Released two days before America's 250th birthday, the compilation spans motel lobbies, yoga studios, Fortune 500 boardrooms — and asks who still gets left out of the story.
articles.image_caption: M.R. Rangaswami, founder and chairman of Indiaspora, at a diaspora event
articles.nri_angle: A definitive compilation of how Indian Americans have shaped the United States across 15 domains — from hospitality and tech to philanthropy and civil rights — released as America marks its semiquincentennial.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Modi Is Taking His Diaspora Playbook to Three Countries in Six Days. In One of Them, It Will Be Tested.
articles.excerpt: A million Indians in Australia, a 40-year gap in New Zealand, and the 'butter chicken tsunami' that won't go away — inside the Indo-Pacific tour that starts Monday.
articles.image_caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi, whose six-day Indo-Pacific tour begins July 6
articles.nri_angle: Modi's three-nation tour includes large-scale diaspora addresses in every stop, but the NZ leg puts a spotlight on rising anti-Indian sentiment and hate crimes that have left the community feeling targeted.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: They Started Fighting for India in Westminster During the Emergency. Fifty Years Later, They Want Blue Plaques.
articles.excerpt: FISI UK, the oldest Indian advocacy organisation in Britain, celebrated its golden jubilee with a new initiative to map every Indian trailblazer who lived on British soil.
articles.image_caption: The Bhavan Indian Arts Centre in West Kensington, London — venue for the FISI UK Golden Jubilee
articles.nri_angle: FISI UK was founded by British Indians in 1976 to give the diaspora a political voice in Westminster. Its 50-year journey mirrors the trajectory of the British Indian community itself — from political invisibility to mainstream influence. The SMRITI initiative now aims to preserve that history for future generations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Duke Cardiologists Now Lead the American Heart Association. Both Are Children of Indian Immigrants.
articles.excerpt: Dr. Manesh Patel becomes the first South Asian to serve as AHA volunteer president. His president-elect, Dr. Svati Shah, runs one of the country's leading precision cardiovascular genetics programmes. Both start July 1.
articles.image_caption: Duke Chapel on the Duke University campus in Durham, North Carolina — home institution of Dr. Manesh Patel and Dr. Svati Shah, now leading the American Heart Association
articles.nri_angle: Two Indian-American doctors simultaneously leading the AHA marks a generational milestone for a community that is overrepresented in medicine but underrepresented in legacy medical leadership. South Asians also face disproportionately high cardiovascular risk, making this appointment personally significant for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: New Zealand Signed a Trade Deal With India. Then It Quietly Started Writing Immigration Rules That Apply to Indians — and Only Indians.
articles.excerpt: Even NZ's own Foreign Minister calls the proposed restrictions discriminatory. Days before Modi's first-ever visit, the country's coalition government is tearing itself apart over who gets to come in.
articles.image_caption: New Zealand's Parliament House in Wellington, where the ruling coalition is divided over immigration rules that single out Indian nationals under the newly signed free trade agreement.
articles.nri_angle: New Zealand's proposed immigration restrictions specifically target Indian nationals, affecting NRI workers, students, and the 250,000-strong Indian diaspora community — with racist rhetoric and anti-Indian protests compounding the policy threat
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The USISPF Summit Honoured Three Business Titans. Sunil Mittal Used His Speech to Talk About Five Million Indians Instead.
articles.excerpt: At the IX USISPF Leadership Summit in Washington, Bharti's chairman and India's ambassador to the US laid out a vision in which the diaspora is not a footnote to the India-US partnership but the load-bearing wall.
articles.image_caption: Sunil Bharti Mittal, founder and chairman of Bharti Enterprises
articles.nri_angle: Mittal explicitly framed the 5-million-strong Indian American community as the strategic bridge between India and the US — in trade, defence, and high technology. Ambassador Kwatra's $30 trillion roadmap positions the diaspora as investors, knowledge partners, and connectors in India's climb to developed-nation status by 2047.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sitharaman Took India's Chequebook to France. She Is Ending the Trip by Meeting the Diaspora.
articles.excerpt: India's finance minister co-chaired an economic dialogue in Aix-en-Provence, courted BNP Paribas and a cargo airship startup, and will wrap up her four-day visit with a community event for Indians in France — the quiet end of a loud trip.
articles.image_caption: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman during a European engagement in 2025
articles.nri_angle: Sitharaman's France visit concludes with a diaspora community interaction, connecting India's economic diplomacy directly to the 30,000-strong Indian community in France. India-France trade has doubled in a decade to €13.59 billion, and the India-EU FTA signed in January 2026 opens new pathways for NRIs across Europe.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indian Immigrants Have Built 96 Billion-Dollar Startups in America. No Other Country Comes Close.
articles.excerpt: A new NFAP study finds India is the largest source of immigrant unicorn founders in the US, with 96 companies collectively worth more than Germany's stock market.
articles.image_caption: Jyoti Bansal, Indian-born founder of AppDynamics and Harness, at TechCrunch Disrupt 2024 — one of 96 Indian immigrant-founded US unicorn startups identified in the NFAP study (Photo: TechCrunch/Katelyn Tucker, CC BY 2.0)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-born entrepreneurs account for 96 of America's 775 unicorns — the most of any country. Most arrived as IIT graduates on student visas, building the exact pipeline now threatened by tightening H-1B and student visa policies.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Carnegie Names Four Indian Americans to Its 'Great Immigrants' List — on the Eve of America's 250th Birthday
articles.excerpt: Nikesh Arora, Mahzarin Banaji, Sanjiv Chopra, and Reshma Kewalramani join a class of 25 naturalized citizens honoured by the Carnegie Corporation for the Fourth of July.
articles.image_caption: Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, one of four Indian Americans named to Carnegie's 2026 Great Immigrants list
articles.nri_angle: Four Indian-born leaders — spanning cybersecurity, social psychology, medicine, and biotech — are honoured as 'Great Americans' at a moment when immigration restrictions are tightening. The recognition underscores the diaspora's institutional reach across American life.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: New US Bill Would End OPT, Kill H-1B Green Card Pathway in Sweeping Overhaul
articles.excerpt: Rep. Chip Roy’s American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act targets every stage of the Indian professional immigration pipeline, from student work permits to permanent residency
articles.image_caption: The US Capitol, where Rep. Chip Roy introduced the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026 targeting the H-1B visa program.
articles.nri_angle: Indians hold 72% of H-1B visas and rely on OPT and the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline that this bill would dismantle — a direct threat to the immigration pathway used by hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
